claim: Two rhesus macaques were trained to perform a rule-based category-response task.
source: Two rhesus macaques were trained to perform a rule-based category-response task.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: On each trial, monkeys were presented with a stimulus composed of a color and shape.
source: On each trial, the monkeys were presented with a stimulus that was composed of a color and shape (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the task design and references Figure 1a showing the trial structure.

claim: The shape and color of each stimulus were drawn from a continuous space.
source: The shape and color of each stimulus were drawn from a continuous space and, depending on the current rule in effect, the animals categorized the stimulus according to either its color (red vs. green) or its shape ('bunny' vs.'tee', Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this in the task description and references Figure 1b.

claim: Animals categorized stimuli according to either color (red vs. green) or shape ('bunny' vs. 'tee') depending on the current rule.
source: The shape and color of each stimulus were drawn from a continuous space and, depending on the current rule in effect, the animals categorized the stimulus according to either its color (red vs. green) or its shape ('bunny' vs.'tee', Figure 1b).
evidence: The task design explicitly describes the categorization requirements.

claim: Animals were trained on three different category-response rules.
source: Animals were trained on three different category-response rules (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task design section.

claim: Rule 1 required the animal to categorize the shape of the stimulus, making a saccade to the upper-left location when the shape was categorized as a 'bunny' and a saccade to the lower-right location when the shape was categorized as a 'tee'.
source: Rule 1 required the animal to categorize the shape of the stimulus, making a saccade to the upper-left location when the shape was categorized as a 'bunny' and a saccade to the lower-right location when the shape was categorized as a 'tee'.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes Rule 1 in the task design.

claim: Rule 2 required the animal to categorize the color of the stimulus and respond on Axis 2 (red = upper-right, green = lower-left).
source: Rule 2 was similar but required the animal to categorize the color of the stimulus and then respond on the opposite axis (Axis 2; red = upper-right, green = lower-left).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes Rule 2 in the task design.

claim: Rule 3 required categorizing the color of the stimulus and responding on Axis 1 (red = lower-right, green = upper-left).
source: Finally, Rule 3 required categorizing the color of the stimulus and responding on Axis 1 (red = lower-right, green = upper-left).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes Rule 3 in the task design.

claim: The rules are compositional in nature, with overlapping dimensions.
source: Note that these rules are compositional in nature, with overlapping dimensions (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this and references Figure 1d showing the overlap.

claim: Rule 1 required categorizing the shape of the stimulus, while Rules 2 and 3 required categorizing the color of the stimulus.
source: Rule 1 required categorizing the shape of the stimulus, while Rules 2 and 3 required categorizing the color of the stimulus.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: Rules 1 and 3 required responding on the same axis (Axis 1), while Rule 2 required a different set of responses (Axis 2).
source: Similarly, Rules 1 and 3 required responding on the same axis (Axis 1), while Rule 2 required a different set of responses (Axis 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: The overlap in the response axis for Rules 1 and 3 meant certain stimuli had congruent responses for both rules while other stimuli had incongruent responses between rules.
source: In addition, the overlap in the response axis for Rules 1 and 3 meant certain stimuli had congruent responses for both rules (e.g., red-tee and green-bunny stimuli) while other stimuli had incongruent responses between rules (e.g., red-bunny and green-tee).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: When the animal made a correct response, it received a reward; an incorrect response led to a short 'time-out'.
source: For all rules, when the animal made a correct response, it received a reward (an incorrect response led to a short 'time-out').
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: Animals performed the same rule during a block of trials.
source: Animals performed the same rule during a block of trials.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: The animals were not explicitly cued as to which rule was in effect for that block.
source: Critically, the animals were not explicitly cued as to which rule was in effect for that block.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: Animals had to use information about the stimulus, their response, and reward feedback to infer which rule was in effect.
source: Instead, they had to use information about the stimulus, their response, and reward feedback, to infer which rule was in effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: After the animals discovered the rule and were performing it at a high level (>70%), the rule would switch.
source: After the animals discovered the rule and were performing it at a high level (defined as >70%, see Methods) the rule would switch.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: The moment of switching rules was cued to the animals with a flashing screen.
source: Although unpredictable, the moment of switching rules was cued to the animals (with a flashing screen).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: The switch cue did not indicate which rule was now in effect, just that a switch had occurred.
source: Importantly, this switch cue did not indicate which rule was now in effect (just that a switch had occurred).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: The sequence of rules across blocks was semi-structured such that the axis of response always changed following a block switch.
source: To facilitate learning and performance, the sequence of rules across blocks was semi-structured such that the axis of response always changed following a block switch.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: The animals always alternated between a Rule 2 block and either a Rule 1 or 3 block (chosen pseudo randomly).
source: This means that the animals always alternated between a Rule 2 block and either a Rule 1 or 3 block (chosen pseudo randomly), and that Rule 2 thus occurred twice as frequently as the other rules.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: Rule 2 occurred twice as frequently as the other rules.
source: This means that the animals always alternated between a Rule 2 block and either a Rule 1 or 3 block (chosen pseudo randomly), and that Rule 2 thus occurred twice as frequently as the other rules.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the task description.

claim: Both monkeys performed the task well above chance.
source: Overall, both monkeys performed the task well above chance (Figure 1e, f).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1e, f.

claim: When the rule switched to Rule 2, Monkey S responded correctly on the first trial in 81% of Rule 2 blocks.
source: When the rule switched to Rule 2, the animals quickly switched their behavior: Monkey S responded correctly on the first trial in 81%, confidence interval (CI) = [0.74,0.87] of Rule 2 blocks, and reached 91%, CI = [0.85,0.95] after only 20 trials (Monkey C being, respectively, at 78%, CI = [0.65,0.88]; and 85%, CI = [0.72,0.92]).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey S reached 91% correct performance after only 20 trials in Rule 2.
source: When the rule switched to Rule 2, the animals quickly switched their behavior: Monkey S responded correctly on the first trial in 81%, confidence interval (CI) = [0.74,0.87] of Rule 2 blocks, and reached 91%, CI = [0.85,0.95] after only 20 trials (Monkey C being, respectively, at 78%, CI = [0.65,0.88]; and 85%, CI = [0.72,0.92]).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey C responded correctly on the first trial in 78% of Rule 2 blocks.
source: When the rule switched to Rule 2, the animals quickly switched their behavior: Monkey S responded correctly on the first trial in 81%, confidence interval (CI) = [0.74,0.87] of Rule 2 blocks, and reached 91%, CI = [0.85,0.95] after only 20 trials (Monkey C being, respectively, at 78%, CI = [0.65,0.88]; and 85%, CI = [0.72,0.92]).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey C reached 85% correct performance after 20 trials in Rule 2.
source: When the rule switched to Rule 2, the animals quickly switched their behavior: Monkey S responded correctly on the first trial in 81%, confidence interval (CI) = [0.74,0.87] of Rule 2 blocks, and reached 91%, CI = [0.85,0.95] after only 20 trials (Monkey C being, respectively, at 78%, CI = [0.65,0.88]; and 85%, CI = [0.72,0.92]).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: In Rule 1, Monkey S's performance was below chance on the first trial (0%), reflecting perseveration on the previous rule.
source: In Rule 1, although the performance of Monkey S was below chance on the first trial (0%, CI = [0,0.052]; 46%, CI = [0.28,0.65] for Monkey C), reflecting perseveration on the previous rule, performance quickly climbed above chance (77% after 50 trials, CI = [0.66,0.85]; 63%, CI = [0.43,0.79] for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey S's performance in Rule 1 quickly climbed above chance to 77% after 50 trials.
source: In Rule 1, although the performance of Monkey S was below chance on the first trial (0%, CI = [0,0.052]; 46%, CI = [0.28,0.65] for Monkey C), reflecting perseveration on the previous rule, performance quickly climbed above chance (77% after 50 trials, CI = [0.66,0.85]; 63%, CI = [0.43,0.79] for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey C's performance in Rule 1 was 46% on the first trial.
source: In Rule 1, although the performance of Monkey S was below chance on the first trial (0%, CI = [0,0.052]; 46%, CI = [0.28,0.65] for Monkey C), reflecting perseveration on the previous rule, performance quickly climbed above chance (77% after 50 trials, CI = [0.66,0.85]; 63%, CI = [0.43,0.79] for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey C's performance in Rule 1 reached 63% after 50 trials.
source: In Rule 1, although the performance of Monkey S was below chance on the first trial (0%, CI = [0,0.052]; 46%, CI = [0.28,0.65] for Monkey C), reflecting perseveration on the previous rule, performance quickly climbed above chance (77% after 50 trials, CI = [0.66,0.85]; 63%, CI = [0.43,0.79] for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: A similar pattern of performance was seen for Rule 3, with Monkey S showing initial performance of 1.5% and 78% after 50 trials.
source: A similar pattern was seen for Rule 3 (initial performance of 1.5%, CI = [0.0026,0.079] and 78%, CI = [0.67,0.86] after 50 trials for Monkey S; 41%, CI = [0.25,0.59] and 67%, CI = [0.48,0.81] for Monkey C, respectively).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey C showed initial performance of 41% in Rule 3 and 67% after 50 trials.
source: A similar pattern was seen for Rule 3 (initial performance of 1.5%, CI = [0.0026,0.079] and 78%, CI = [0.67,0.86] after 50 trials for Monkey S; 41%, CI = [0.25,0.59] and 67%, CI = [0.48,0.81] for Monkey C, respectively).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: The monkeys were slower to switch to Rules 1 and 3 than to switch to Rule 2.
source: First, the monkeys were slower to switch to Rules 1 and 3 than to switch to Rule 2.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a behavioral observation.

claim: On the first 20 trials, the difference in average percent performance of Monkey S was Δ = 35 between Rules 2 and 1, and Δ = 22 between Rules 2 and 3.
source: On the first 20 trials, the difference in average percent performance of Monkey S was Δ = 35 between Rules 2 and 1, and Δ = 22 between Rules 2 and 3 (significant Fisher's test comparing Rule 2 to Rules 1 and 3, with p < 10−4 in both conditions; respectively, Δ = 35, Δ = 24 and p < 10−4 for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical significance provided.

claim: The difference in performance between Rule 2 and Rules 1 and 3 was statistically significant (Fisher's test p < 10−4).
source: On the first 20 trials, the difference in average percent performance of Monkey S was Δ = 35 between Rules 2 and 1, and Δ = 22 between Rules 2 and 3 (significant Fisher's test comparing Rule 2 to Rules 1 and 3, with p < 10−4 in both conditions; respectively, Δ = 35, Δ = 24 and p < 10−4 for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results.

claim: Both monkeys learned the axis of response nearly instantaneously.
source: Second, both monkeys learned the axis of response nearly instantaneously.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a behavioral observation.

claim: After a switch cue, Monkey S almost always responded on Axis 2 (97% in Rule 1, 97% in Rule 2, 97% in Rule 3).
source: After a switch cue, Monkey S almost always responded on Axis 2 (the response axis consistent with Rule 2; 97%, CI = [0.90,0.99] in Rule 1; 97%, CI = [0.92,0.98] in Rule 2; 97%, CI = [0.90,0.99] in Rule 3; see Figure 1g).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals and references Figure 1g.

claim: If the initial Axis 2 response was incorrect, Monkey S switched to the correct axis within five trials on 97% of blocks of Rule 1 and 94% of blocks of Rule 3.
source: Then, if this was incorrect, it switched to the correct axis within five trials on 97%, CI = [0.90,0.99] of blocks of Rule 1, and 94% CI = [0.86,0.98] of blocks of Rule 3.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Monkey C tended to alternate the response axis on the first trial following a switch cue.
source: Monkey C instead tended to alternate the response axis on the first trial following a switch cue (it made a response on the correct axis on the first trial with a probability of 71%, CI = [0.51,0.85] in Rule 1; 85%, CI = [0.72,0.92] in Rule 2; and 84%, CI = [0.55,0.87] in Rule 3), implying an understanding of the pattern of axis changes with block switches (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals and references Figure 1h.

claim: Monkey C made a response on the correct axis on the first trial with a probability of 71% in Rule 1, 85% in Rule 2, and 84% in Rule 3.
source: Monkey C instead tended to alternate the response axis on the first trial following a switch cue (it made a response on the correct axis on the first trial with a probability of 71%, CI = [0.51,0.85] in Rule 1; 85%, CI = [0.72,0.92] in Rule 2; and 84%, CI = [0.55,0.87] in Rule 3), implying an understanding of the pattern of axis changes with block switches (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: Both monkeys maintained the correct axis with very few off-axis responses throughout the block.
source: Both monkeys maintained the correct axis with very few off-axis responses throughout the block (at trial 20, Monkey S: 1.4%, CI = [0.0025,0.077] in Rule 1; 2.1%, CI = [0.0072,0.060] in Rule 2; 0%, CI = [0,0.053] in Rule 3; Monkey C: 0%, CI = [0,0.14] in Rule 1; 4.3%, CI = [0.012,0.15] in Rule 2; 3.7%, CI = [0.0066,0.18] in Rule 3).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals provided.

claim: The animals were able to quickly identify the axis of response but took longer to learn the correct mapping between stimulus features and responses within an axis.
source: These results suggest the animals were able to quickly identify the axis of response but took longer (particularly for Rules 1 and 3) to learn the correct mapping between stimulus features and responses within an axis.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: An error-driven learning model (QL) was fit to the monkeys' behavior.
source: First, we fit an error-driven learning model, which gradually relearns the stimulus–response mappings de novo at the start of each block, to the monkeys' behavior.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the modeling section.

claim: The QL model uses incremental running averages to smooth out trial-to-trial stochasticity in reward realization.
source: This class of models works by learning the reward expected for different stimulus–response combinations, using incremental running averages to smooth out trial-to-trial stochasticity in reward realization – here, due to perceptual noise in the stimulus classification.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the model description.

claim: The QL model was unable to match the animals' ability to rapidly switch axes.
source: Yet, even with these built-in advantages, the model was unable to match the animals' ability to rapidly switch axes, but instead relearned the feature–response associations after each block switch (simulations under best-fitting parameters shown in Figure 2 for Monkey S, Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: The QL model fitted on Monkey S's behavior responded on Axis 2 on the first trial of the block only 50% of the time in all three rules.
source: For instance, the model fitted on Monkey S's behavior responded on Axis 2 on the first trial of the block only 50% of the time in all three rules (Figure 2a, Fisher's test of model simulations against data: p < 10−4 for the three rules).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results and references Figure 2a.

claim: The QL model switched to the correct axis within five trials on only 58% of blocks of Rule 1 and 57% of blocks of Rule 3.
source: Importantly, the model switched to the correct axis within five trials on only 58% of blocks of Rule 1, and 57% of blocks of Rule 3 (Figure 2b, Fisher's test against monkey behavior: p < 10−4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results and references Figure 2b.

claim: The QL model performed 24% of off-axis responses after 20 trials in Rule 1, 21% in Rule 2, and 21% in Rule 3, all much higher than observed in the monkey's behavior.
source: Finally, the model performed 24% of off-axis responses after 20 trials in Rule 1, 21% in Rule 2, and 21% in Rule 3, all much higher than what was observed in the monkey's behavior (Fisher's test p < 10−4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results.

claim: A fully informed Bayesian ideal observer model (IO) uses statistical inference to continually estimate which of the three rules is in effect.
source: A fully informed Bayesian ideal observer model (IO, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Methods) uses statistical inference to continually estimate which of the three rules is in effect, accumulating evidence ('beliefs') for each rule based on the history of previous stimuli, actions, and rewards.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the model description.

claim: The IO model chooses the optimal action for any given stimulus by averaging the associated actions' values under each rule, weighted by the estimated likelihood that each rule is in effect.
source: The IO model chooses the optimal action for any given stimulus, by averaging the associated actions' values under each rule, weighted by the estimated likelihood that each rule is in effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the model description.

claim: The IO model predicts the speed of initial (re)learning after a block switch should be coupled to the asymptotic level of performance.
source: Indeed, the IO model predicts the speed of initial (re)learning after a block switch should be coupled to the asymptotic level of performance.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a prediction of the IO model.

claim: The IO model reproduced the animals' ability to rapidly infer the correct axis.
source: As expected, when fit to the animal's behavior, the IO model reproduced the animals' ability to rapidly infer the correct axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, b, d, e).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: The IO model could not capture the observed differences in learning speed for the different rules.
source: However, the IO model could not capture the observed differences in learning speed for the different rules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, f).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: The monkey's performance depended on how difficult it was to categorize the stimulus (i.e., the morph level).
source: As expected, the monkey's performance depended on how difficult it was to categorize the stimulus (i.e., the morph level; psychometric curves shown in Figure 3a–c for Monkey S, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by psychometric curves shown in figures.

claim: On early trials of Rule 2, Monkey S correctly responded to 96% of prototype stimuli and only to 91% of 'morphed' stimuli.
source: Indeed, on 'early trials' (first 50 trials) of Rule 2, Monkey S correctly responded to 96% (CI = [0.95,0.97]) of prototype stimuli, and only to 91%, CI = [0.90,0.92] of 'morphed' stimuli (p < 10−4; similar results for Monkey C in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals and statistical significance.

claim: There was a discrepancy between the performance on 'morphed' stimuli in Rule 2 versus Rule 3, with a difference in average percent performance of Δ = 28 for the first 50 trials in both rules.
source: Importantly, there was a discrepancy between the performance on 'morphed' stimuli in Rule 2 versus Rule 3, with a difference in average percent performance of Δ = 28 for the first 50 trials in both rules (p < 10−4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical significance.

claim: The IO model performed similarly for morphed stimuli on Rules 2 and 3 because both rules involve categorizing color and so they shared the same perceptual noise.
source: However, the model performed similarly for morphed stimuli on Rules 2 and 3. This is because both rules involve categorizing color and so they shared the same perceptual noise, leading to the same likelihood of errors.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an explanation for the model's behavior.

claim: Using best-fit parameters, the IO model reproduced the animals' lower asymptotic performance in Rule 3 by increasing color noise, and so it failed to capture the high performance on Rule 2 early on.
source: Using best-fit parameters, the model reproduced the animals' lower asymptotic performance in Rule 3 by increasing color noise, and so it failed to capture the high performance on Rule 2 early on (Figure 3e, f, Figure 3—figure supplement 2e, f).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: A hybrid model (HQL) that inferred the axis of response while incrementally learning which features to attend for that response axis was implemented.
source: To test this hypothesis, we implemented a hybrid model that inferred the axis of response while incrementally learning which features to attend for that response axis (Hybrid Q Learner, 'HQL' in the Methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the model description.

claim: In the HQL model, the current axis of response was inferred through Bayesian evidence accumulation, while feature–response weights were incrementally learned for each axis of response.
source: In the model, the current axis of response was inferred through Bayesian evidence accumulation (as in the IO model), while feature–response weights were incrementally learned for each axis of response.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the model description.

claim: The HQL model provided an accurate account of the animals' behavior.
source: Consistent with this intuition, the HQL model provided an accurate account of the animals' behavior.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a summary of the model results.

claim: The HQL model reproduced the fast switch to the correct axis.
source: First, unlike the QL model, the HQL model reproduced the fast switch to the correct axis (Figure 4a, b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, bCited, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–c and g–i).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: Fitted to Monkey S behavior, the HQL model initially responded on Axis 2 immediately after each block switch cue (91% in Rule 1, 89% in Rules 2 and 3).
source: Fitted to Monkey S behavior, the model initially responded on Axis 2 immediately after each block switch cue (91% in Rule 1, 89% in Rules 2 and 3, Fisher's test against monkey's behavior p > 0.05).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results.

claim: The HQL model captured the animals' fast performance on Rule 2 and slower performance on Rules 1 and 3.
source: Second, contrary to the IO model, the HQL model captured the animals' fast performance on Rule 2 and slower performance on Rules 1 and 3 (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: Fitted on Monkey S's behavior, the HQL model showed a difference in average percent performance on the first 20 trials of Δ = 31 between Rules 2 and 1, and Δ = 29 between Rules 2 and 3.
source: The model captured this difference: fitted on Monkey S's behavior, the difference in average percent performance on the first 20 trials was Δ = 31 between Rules 2 and 1, and Δ = 29 between Rules 2 and 3 (a Fisher's test against monkey's behavior gave p > 0.05 for the first trial, p > 0.1 for trial 20).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results.

claim: The HQL model captured the trade-off between the animals' initial learning rate and asymptotic behavioral performance in Rules 2 and 3.
source: Third, the HQL model captured the trade-off between the animals' initial learning rate and asymptotic behavioral performance in Rules 2 and 3 (Figure 4d–f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: The animals performed better on congruent stimuli than incongruent stimuli.
source: Consistent with previous work (Noppeney et al., 2010; Venkatraman et al., 2009; Bugg et al., 2008; Carter et al., 1995; Musslick and Cohen, 2021), the animals performed better on congruent stimuli than incongruent stimuli (Figure 5a for Monkey S, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to previous work and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: During early trials of Rules 1 and 3, the monkeys' performance was significantly higher for congruent stimuli than for incongruent stimuli (94% vs. 57% for Monkey S).
source: This effect was strongest during learning, but persisted throughout the block (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a, e): during early trials of Rules 1 and 3, the monkeys' performance was significantly higher for congruent stimuli than for incongruent stimuli (gray vs. red squares in Figure 5b; 94%, CI = [0.93,0.95] vs. 57%, CI = [0.55,0.58], respectively; Δ = 37, Fisher's test p < 10−4; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1b for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals and statistical significance.

claim: The animals were slower to respond to incongruent stimuli (Δ = 25 ms in reaction time for incongruent and congruent stimuli).
source: Similarly, the animals were slower to respond to incongruent stimuli (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Δ = 25 ms in reaction time for incongruent and congruent stimuli, t-test, p < 10−4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results and references a figure.

claim: The congruency of stimuli had no effect during Rule 2 – behavior depended only on the stimulus color.
source: In contrast, the congruency of stimuli had no effect during Rule 2 – behavior depended only on the stimulus color, suggesting the monkeys ignored the shape of the stimulus during Rule 2, even when the morph level of the color was more difficult (gray vs. red squares in Figure 5c; performance was 92%, CI = [0.90,0.93], and 93%, CI = [0.92,0.93] for congruent and incongruent stimuli, respectively; with Δ = −0.73; Fisher's test, p = 0.40; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1c for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with confidence intervals and statistical test results.

claim: Pure incremental learning by the QL model did not capture the incongruency effect, but instead predicted an opposite effect.
source: First, pure incremental learning by the QL model did not capture this result, but instead predicted an opposite effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model result.

claim: Incongruent trials were four times more likely than congruent trials.
source: This is because incongruent trials were four times more likely than congruent trials (see Methods).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a task design feature.

claim: The QL model fit to Monkey S predicted worse performance on congruent than incongruent trials (45% and 62%, respectively).
source: As the QL model encodes the statistics of the task through error-driven updating of action values, the proportion of congruent versus incongruent trials led to an anti-incongruency effect – the QL model fit to Monkey S predicted worse performance on congruent than incongruent trials (Figure 5d, e; 45% and 62%, respectively; Δ = −16; Fisher's test p < 10−4; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1d, e for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results and references figures.

claim: The IO model also did not capture the incongruency effect.
source: Second, the IO model also did not capture the incongruency effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model result.

claim: Learning in the IO model quickly reached asymptotic performance for both congruent and incongruent trials (75% and 72%, respectively).
source: However, given the statistics of the task, learning in the IO model quickly reached asymptotic performance, for both congruent and incongruent trials (Figure 5g, h; 75% and 72%, respectively; Δ = 3.8 only; Figure 5—figure supplement 1g, h for Monkey C), hence not reproducing the incongruency effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: The hybrid HQL model captured the incongruency effect.
source: In contrast to the QL and IO models, the hybrid HQL model captured the incongruency effect.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model result.

claim: In the HQL model, the weights for mapping congruent stimuli to responses were the same for Rules 1 and 3.
source: In the HQL model, the weights for mapping congruent stimuli to responses were the same for Rules 1 and 3.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a property of the HQL model.

claim: In the HQL model, the weights for incongruent stimuli must change for Rules 1 and 3.
source: In contrast, the weights for incongruent stimuli must change for Rules 1 and 3.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a property of the HQL model.

claim: The HQL model fitted to Monkey S behavior reproduced the greater performance on congruent than incongruent stimuli (92% and 61%, respectively).
source: The model fitted to Monkey S behavior reproduced the greater performance on congruent than incongruent stimuli (Figure 5g, h; 92% and 61%, respectively, Δ = 31; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1g, h for Monkey C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by model simulations shown in figures.

claim: Only a hybrid model performing both rule switching of axis and rule learning of features could account for the incongruency effect observed in the behavior.
source: As a result, only a hybrid model performing both rule switching of axis and rule learning of features could account for the incongruency effect observed in the behavior.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Rule switching and rule learning rely on distinct but intertwined computations, namely fast inference and slower incremental learning.
source: Here, we show these two processes, rule switching and rule learning, rely on distinct but intertwined computations, namely fast inference and slower incremental learning.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The animals learned the axis of response using fast inference (rule switching) while continuously re-estimating the stimulus–response associations within an axis (rule learning).
source: By modeling behavior, we found the animals learned the axis of response using fast inference (rule switching) while continuously re-estimating the stimulus–response associations within an axis (rule learning).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Error-driven learning rules are associated with dopamine and the basal ganglia.
source: A long tradition of research in areas like Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning has focused on elucidating general-purpose trial-and-error learning mechanisms – especially error-driven learning rules associated with dopamine and the basal ganglia (Daw and O'Doherty, 2014; Daw and Shohamy, 2008; Daw and Tobler, 2014; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Doya, 2007; O'Doherty et al., 2004; O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Rescorla, 1988; Schultz et al., 1997; Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Day et al., 2007; Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Lau and Glimcher, 2008; Samejima et al., 2005; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: If two different stimulus–response rules are repeatedly reinforced in alternation, animals can come to switch between them more rapidly.
source: However, in other circumstances, learning can also be quicker and more specialized: for instance, if two different stimulus–response rules are repeatedly reinforced in alternation, animals can come to switch between them more rapidly (Asaad et al., 1998; Rougier et al., 2005; Harlow, 1949).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Task-specialized dynamics are often modeled by Bayesian latent state inference, where animals accumulate evidence about which of several 'latent' rules currently applies.
source: These more task-specialized dynamics are often modeled by a distinct computational mechanism, such as Bayesian latent state inference, where animals accumulate evidence about which of several 'latent' (i.e., not directly observable) rules currently applies (Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019; Collins and Koechlin, 2012; Behrens et al., 2007; Gershman et al., 2014; Bartolo and Averbeck, 2020; Qi et al., 2022; Stoianov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Latent state inference is associated with activity in the prefrontal cortex.
source: Such inference is associated with activity in the prefrontal cortex (Durstewitz et al., 2010; Milner, 1963; Boettiger and D'Esposito, 2005; Nakahara et al., 2002; Genovesio et al., 2005; Boorman et al., 2009; Koechlin and Hyafil, 2007; Koechlin et al., 2003; Sakai and Passingham, 2003; Badre et al., 2010; Miller and Cohen, 2001; Antzoulatos and Miller, 2011; Reinert et al., 2021; Mansouri et al., 2020), suggesting that its neural mechanisms are distinct from incremental learning.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Lesioning prefrontal cortex impairs performance on tasks that require rule inference.
source: Lesioning prefrontal cortex impairs performance on tasks that require rule inference (Milner, 1963; Dias et al., 1996) and neurons in prefrontal cortex track the currently inferred rule (Mansouri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in prefrontal cortex track the currently inferred rule.
source: Lesioning prefrontal cortex impairs performance on tasks that require rule inference (Milner, 1963; Dias et al., 1996) and neurons in prefrontal cortex track the currently inferred rule (Mansouri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with a citation to prior literature.

claim: Latent state inference presupposes that the animals have previously learned about the structure of the task.
source: In its simplest form, this type of latent state inference process presupposes that the animals have previously learned about the structure of the task.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a property of latent state inference models.

claim: Latent state inference has typically been studied in well-trained animals.
source: For this reason, latent state inference has typically been studied in well-trained animals (Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019; Asaad et al., 2000; White and Wise, 1999).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: One solution to latent state learning is that rule learning and rule switching involve an interaction between latent state inference and incremental trial-and-error learning.
source: Perhaps most intriguingly, one solution to the lack of a full process-level model of latent state learning is that rule learning and rule switching involve an interaction between both major classes of learning mechanisms – latent state inference and incremental trial-and-error learning.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a theoretical proposal.

claim: In Bayesian inference models, it is often hypothesized that an inferential process decides which latent state is in effect (e.g., in prefrontal cortex), while the properties of each state are learned by downstream error-driven incremental learning (e.g, in the striatum).
source: Thus, in Bayesian inference models, it is often hypothesized that an inferential process decides which latent state is in effect (e.g., in prefrontal cortex), while the properties of each state are learned, conditional on this, by downstream error-driven incremental learning (e.g, in the striatum) (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Collins and Koechlin, 2012; Frank and Badre, 2012; Seo et al., 2012; Rushworth et al., 2011; Balewski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: The two learning mechanisms (inference and incremental learning) have mostly been studied in regimes where they operate in isolation.
source: However, these two learning mechanisms have mostly been studied in regimes where they operate in isolation (Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019; Asaad et al., 2000; White and Wise, 1999; Lak et al., 2020; Busse et al., 2011; Fründ et al., 2014; Gold et al., 2008; Tsunada et al., 2019) and, apart from a few examples in human rule learning (Collins and Koechlin, 2012; Collins and Frank, 2016; Donoso et al., 2014; Badre and Frank, 2012; Bouchacourt et al., 2020; Franklin and Frank, 2018), their interaction has been limited to theoretical work.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior literature.

claim: All models shared common noisy perceptual input and action selection stages.
source: As in previous work (Dayan and Daw, 2008; Pouget et al., 2016; Pouget et al., 2013; Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Bichot and Schall, 1999), all our models shared common noisy perceptual input and action selection stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Methods).

claim: All models were fitted with Monte Carlo Markov chains (MCMC) using Stan.
source: Because of noise perception at each trial, and because the cumulative distribution function of a Von Mises is not analytic, the models are fitted with Monte Carlo Markov chains (MCMC) using Stan (Carpenter, 2017).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Methods section with a citation.

claim: Each day of recording was fitted separately.
source: Each day of recording is fitted separately, and the mean and standard deviation reported in Table 1 are between days.

claim: Convergence was validated by monitoring the potential scale reduction factor R-hat (which was <1.05 for all simulations) and an estimate of the effective sample size (all effective sample sizes >100).
source: We validated convergence by monitoring the potential scale reduction factor R-hat (which was <1.05 for all simulations) and an estimate of the effective sample size (all effective sample sizes >100) of the models' fits (Gelman and Rubin, 1992).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Methods section with a citation.

claim: The results make testable neural predictions that there should be two latent states represented in the brain.
source: First, our results make the strong prediction that there should be two latent states represented in the brain – the representation for the two rules competing on one axis (Rules 1 and 3) should be more similar to one another than to the neural representation of the rule alone on the other axis (Rule 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Discussion as a prediction.

claim: The representation for the two rules competing on one axis (Rules 1 and 3) should be more similar to one another than to the neural representation of the rule alone on the other axis (Rule 2).

claim: There may be a functional dissociation for rule switching and rule learning, such that they are represented in distinct networks.
source: Furthermore, our hybrid model suggests there may be a functional dissociation for rule switching and rule learning, such that they are represented in distinct networks.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis.

claim: One hypothesis is that the dissociation between rule switching and rule learning is between cortical and subcortical regions.
source: One hypothesis is that this dissociation is between cortical and subcortical regions.

claim: Prefrontal cortex may carry information about the animal's trial beliefs (i.e., over the two latent states) in a similar manner as perceptual decision making when accumulating evidence from noisy stimuli.
source: Prefrontal cortex may carry information about the animal's trial beliefs (i.e., over the two latent states) in a similar manner as perceptual decision making when accumulating evidence from noisy stimuli (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Shadlen and Kiani, 2013; Rao, 2010; Beck et al., 2008).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis with citations.

claim: Basal ganglia may be engaged in the learning of rule-specific associations.
source: Basal ganglia may, in turn, be engaged in the learning of rule-specific associations (Daw and O'Doherty, 2014; Daw and Shohamy, 2008; Daw and Tobler, 2014; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Doya, 2007; O'Doherty et al., 2004; O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Rescorla, 1988; Schultz et al., 1997; Yin and Knowlton, 2006).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis with citations.

claim: Future work may find both rule switching and rule learning are represented in the same brain regions (e.g., prefrontal cortex).
source: Alternatively, despite their functional dissociation, future work may find both rule switching and rule learning are represented in the same brain regions (e.g., prefrontal cortex).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Discussion as an alternative hypothesis.
